title: Testing, Sanitizers, Static Analysis and Tooling
summary: Professional C++ is supported by tools. **Unit tests** check behaviour. **Sanitizers** catch undefined behaviour as the program runs. **Static analysis** finds defects without running it. **Formatters**, **fuzzers** and **continuous integration** apply all of it to every change.
markdown:
## Layers of defence No single technique finds every defect. Each layer catches what the previous ones missed, and the earlier a problem is caught, the cheaper it is to fix. ```mermaid flowchart LR A["Write code"] --> B["Compiler warnings"] B --> C["Static analysis"] C --> D["Unit tests"] D --> E["Sanitizers"] E --> F["Fuzzing"] F --> G["Continuous integration:
all of it, on every change"] ``` | Layer | Runs the code? | Finds | |---|---|---| | Warnings, static analysis | No | Suspicious patterns on every path, including ones no test exercises | | Unit tests | Yes | Wrong results, for the inputs you thought of | | Sanitizers | Yes | Undefined behaviour on the paths the tests exercise | | Fuzzing | Yes | Failures on inputs you did not think of | ## Unit testing You have been on the receiving end of unit tests throughout this course: every Check in Xenon ran a set of them against your code. [[3.08 Halts, goto, and Testing Your Code]] introduced the idea with a hand-written test function. A **test framework** supplies the infrastructure: registering tests, running them, reporting failures and summarizing. With Catch2: ```cpp #include #include "Fraction.h" TEST_CASE("Fractions reduce automatically", "[fraction]") { const Fraction f{ 2, 4 }; REQUIRE(f.numerator() == 1); REQUIRE(f.denominator() == 2); } TEST_CASE("Adding fractions") { SECTION("the same denominator") { CHECK(Fraction{ 1, 4 } + Fraction{ 2, 4 } == Fraction{ 3, 4 }); } SECTION("a zero denominator throws") { REQUIRE_THROWS_AS(Fraction(1, 0), std::invalid_argument); } } ``` | Macro | On failure | |---|---| | `REQUIRE(expression)` | Reports and stops the current test case | | `CHECK(expression)` | Reports and continues | | `REQUIRE_THROWS_AS(expression, type)` | Fails unless the expression throws that type | GoogleTest is the other widely used framework: `TEST(Fraction, Reduces) { EXPECT_EQ(f.numerator(), 1); }`. The ideas are identical. Either is added to a CMake project with FetchContent ([[10.09 CMake, Libraries and Package Managers]]): ```cmake include(FetchContent) FetchContent_Declare(Catch2 GIT_REPOSITORY https://github.com/catchorg/Catch2.git GIT_TAG v3.7.1) FetchContent_MakeAvailable(Catch2) add_executable(tests tests/test_fraction.cpp) target_link_libraries(tests PRIVATE fraction_lib Catch2::Catch2WithMain) include(CTest) include(Catch) catch_discover_tests(tests) ``` ### What makes code testable | Property | Why | |---|---| | Small, pure functions | The same input always gives the same output, so a test is one line | | Dependencies passed in | A test can supply a fake clock, file system or network: [[8.05 Abstract Classes and Interfaces]] | | No hidden globals | Tests do not interfere with each other: [[13.08 C++ Idioms and Design Patterns]] | | Logic separated from input and output | The logic can be tested without a console or a file | Code that is hard to test is usually code with too many responsibilities or hidden dependencies. The difficulty is design feedback. ### How good are the tests? | Measure | Asks | |---|---| | **Coverage** | Which lines and branches did the tests execute? Uncovered code is untested. Covered code is not necessarily tested **well**. | | **Mutation testing** | If a small bug is introduced deliberately, does any test fail? If not, the tests are not checking that behaviour. | **Test-driven development** reverses the usual order: write a failing test, write the least code that passes it, then tidy up. It guarantees that every piece of behaviour has a test and that the test can fail. ## Sanitizers A **sanitizer** is a compiler option that adds checks to the generated program. The program runs slower and reports errors precisely as they happen. | Sanitizer | Flag (GCC, Clang) | Microsoft | Detects | |---|---|---|---| | AddressSanitizer | `-fsanitize=address` | `/fsanitize=address` | Out-of-bounds access, use after free, double free, leaks | | UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer | `-fsanitize=undefined` | | Signed overflow, bad shifts, null dereference, misalignment | | ThreadSanitizer | `-fsanitize=thread` | | Data races, inconsistent lock ordering | | MemorySanitizer (Clang) | `-fsanitize=memory` | | Reads of uninitialized memory | ```bash g++ -std=c++20 -g -O1 -fsanitize=address,undefined -fno-omit-frame-pointer main.cpp -o app ``` ``` ==12345==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-use-after-free on address 0x602000000010 READ of size 4 at 0x602000000010 thread T0 #0 0x4011a6 in main main.cpp:9 ``` The report names the exact line, and where the memory was allocated and freed. A bug that might have surfaced weeks later as an unrelated crash is pinned down the first time it executes. | Limit | Detail | |---|---| | Only executed code is checked | A sanitizer is as good as the tests that drive it | | Cost | Two to three times slower for ASan; more for TSan | | Combinations | ASan and TSan cannot be used in the same build | The standard practice is to run the whole test suite under ASan and UBSan, and again under TSan for concurrent code. The beaker button above Xenon's editor ("Memory checks") builds your code with AddressSanitizer. ## Static analysis **Static analysis** examines source code without executing it, so it can reason about every path, including error handling that tests rarely reach. | Tool | Notes | |---|---| | Compiler warnings | The first and cheapest analyzer. Turn them up and treat them as errors. | | **clang-tidy** | Hundreds of checks in families: `bugprone-*`, `modernize-*`, `performance-*`, `cppcoreguidelines-*`. Many can fix the code automatically. | | Microsoft Code Analysis | `/analyze`, with a C++ Core Guidelines checker | | cppcheck | Free and standalone | ```yaml # .clang-tidy Checks: 'bugprone-*,modernize-*,performance-*,readability-*,-modernize-use-trailing-return-type' WarningsAsErrors: 'bugprone-*' ``` Static analysis can report problems that are not real (false positives) and cannot find everything. It complements testing; it does not replace it. ## Formatting `clang-format` rewrites code to a style defined in a `.clang-format` file. Format on save, and arguments about brace placement end for good. Code reviews can then be about substance. The wand button above Xenon's editor (or `Shift+Alt+F`) runs it. ## Fuzzing A **fuzzer** calls a function with enormous numbers of generated inputs, guided by which code paths each one reaches, looking for crashes. Combined with sanitizers it is extremely effective on anything that parses untrusted input. ```cpp extern "C" int LLVMFuzzerTestOneInput(const std::uint8_t* data, std::size_t size) { parseConfig(std::string_view{ reinterpret_cast(data), size }); return 0; } ``` ```bash clang++ -fsanitize=fuzzer,address fuzz.cpp parser.cpp ``` You write the single function above; the fuzzer does the rest. ## The debugger A debugger pauses a running program and lets you inspect it. | Feature | Use | |---|---| | Breakpoint | Pause at a line | | **Conditional breakpoint** | Pause only when a condition holds, such as `i == 9999` | | **Data breakpoint** (watchpoint) | Pause when a variable's value **changes**: the fastest way to find who corrupted it | | Call stack | See the chain of calls that led here | | Crash dump | Examine a program's state after it has crashed, on another machine | ## Continuous integration **Continuous integration** (CI) builds the project and runs every check automatically for each change pushed to the repository, on every platform you support. ```yaml jobs: build: strategy: { matrix: { os: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest] } } runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }} steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - run: cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug - run: cmake --build build - run: ctest --test-dir build --output-on-failure ``` The value is that the checks cannot be forgotten. A change that breaks a test, or the build on another platform, is caught within minutes and before it is merged. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? Which sanitizer finds data races? - AddressSanitizer + ThreadSanitizer - UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer - MemorySanitizer > ThreadSanitizer (`-fsanitize=thread`) tracks accesses from different threads. AddressSanitizer finds memory errors such as use-after-free. ? What is the difference between static analysis and a sanitizer? - There is none - Static analysis runs the program; a sanitizer reads the code + Static analysis needs no run; a sanitizer checks while running - Sanitizers only work on Windows > They complement each other: analysers find problems in code that never runs in tests; sanitizers catch real failures in code that does. ? Why does high coverage not prove the tests are good? - Because coverage tools are often wrong - Because coverage counts comments too + It shows code ran, not that a bug there would be caught - Because 100% coverage is impossible > A test with no checks can still run every line. Coverage finds untested code; it does not measure the checks. ? What does a data breakpoint do? - It pauses at a chosen line of code - It logs every variable to a file - It stops the program when it allocates memory + It pauses the program when a particular variable's value changes > Data breakpoints (watchpoints) find the code that modifies a variable unexpectedly. ```
ideas:
1. Take a project of yours and write tests for it in the style of the test function from [[3.08 Halts, goto, and Testing Your Code]], covering every branch.
2. Turn on memory checks with the beaker button and run a memory-management task containing a deliberate use after free.
3. On your own machine, add Catch2 to a CMake project and write twenty tests.

cards.a:
ThreadSanitizer

ThreadSanitizer (`-fsanitize=thread`) tracks accesses from different threads. AddressSanitizer finds memory errors such as use-after-free.

cards.q: What is the difference between static analysis and a sanitizer?
cards.a:
Static analysis needs no run; a sanitizer checks while running

They complement each other: analysers find problems in code that never runs in tests; sanitizers catch real failures in code that does.

cards.q: Why does high coverage not prove the tests are good?
cards.a:
It shows code ran, not that a bug there would be caught

A test with no checks can still run every line. Coverage finds untested code; it does not measure the checks.

cards.q: What does a data breakpoint do?
cards.a:
It pauses the program when a particular variable's value changes

Data breakpoints (watchpoints) find the code that modifies a variable unexpectedly.
